community.headline: Colchester's Provide Community asked to pilot UK nursing public health framework
community.summary: The Colchester-based community health provider has been invited to help test new guidance on how nurses, midwives and nursing associates prevent illness and tackle health inequalities.
body: The Nursing and Midwifery Public Health Practice Framework, published on Monday 16 November 2026 and endorsed by the chief nursing officers of all four UK nations, sets out a shared approach to five areas: promoting wellbeing, protecting people from harm, preventing ill health, reducing inequalities through partnership and environmentally sustainable care. Provide Community announced its part in the pilot on Thursday 19 November.
Professor Lucy Wightman, chief executive of Provide Health and group chief nurse, said a routine appointment can be the first time someone admits they are struggling to manage a condition at home.
points: Framework published on 16 November

community.summary: Tendring's biggest charity Christmas market filled Clacton Town Hall with 26 charity stalls, each keeping the money it took.
body: Shoppers at Clacton Town Hall on Saturday 14 November raised more than £6,000 for charities and good causes at the annual Victorian Christmas Market run by Community Voluntary Services Together (CVST), the Tendring voluntary services charity.

The Salvation Army band played visitors in, volunteers in Victorian dress greeted them at the door, and performers included Young Minds Dementia Choir, Kaleidoscope, SingalongaPen and Princes Youth Theatre. Kevin Burns, of the Clacton branch of Parkinson's UK, won best costume and Grassroots charity won best decorated stall.

It was first shown at the Leigh Art Trail in July and then at Fair Havens' bistro, and explores the hidden feelings children carry when someone important has died.

courts.headline: Danbury man, 79, fined for racially abusing Stansted Airport security
courts.summary: Magistrates in Chelmsford found William Ryan guilty of two counts of racially aggravated harassment after he abused staff at a London Stansted security scanner.
body: Ryan, of Danbury, became abusive after security staff stopped him at a scanner at the airport on 21 June 2025, Hits Radio reports. Witnesses heard him make monkey noises at the staff.

Chelmsford Magistrates' Court convicted him on 28 October. He was fined £1,600 and told to pay £300 compensation and £1,300 costs. Inspector James Southwell of Essex Police said there was no excuse for racially abusing people doing their job.

The offences took place in Harlow between 29 September and 1 October 2025.
As well as the suspended sentence, he must do 150 hours of unpaid work and will be subject to sex offender notification requirements and a Sexual Harm Prevention Order, each for 10 years.

About 20 firefighters, some of them on-call firefighters who live or work within five minutes of their stations, worked to put the fire out. The fire service said no one was aboard the boat at the time.
Crews left the scene at 12.43am on Wednesday 18 November, and the fire service says an investigation will be carried out to establish the cause.

Visitors looking for work, a change of career, seasonal jobs or apprenticeships met employers face to face.

The council ran the fair with the Department for Work and Pensions. Exhibitors included Epping Forest District Museum, Princess Alexandra Hospital's catering service, Lee Valley Regional Park, the Royal Gunpowder Mills, Harlow College, Visit Essex and Delta Hotels by Marriott.

official.headline: Colchester asks residents where to save money in 2027/28 budget
official.summary: Colchester City Council's budget survey runs until 9am on 14 December, with rising homelessness costs among the pressures it lists.
body: Colchester City Council opened its consultation on the 2027/28 budget on Monday 16 November, asking residents where it should cut, spend more or work differently. It names rising costs, steady demand for services and the growing cost of supporting people facing homelessness as the main pressures.

Councillor William Sunnucks, portfolio holder for resources, said: "We need your views on where we can save money." The answers will shape priorities for services including bin collections, parks, leisure, housing and community safety. People can fill in the online survey or attend a Residents' Panel session at the Town Hall from 10am to noon on Tuesday 8 December, or from 7pm to 8.30pm on Thursday 10 December.
Cabinet looks at the first draft budget position on Wednesday 2 December, and the consultation closes at 9am on Monday 14 December. Full Council sets the final budget in February 2027.

body: Colchester United were beaten by Tranmere Rovers in League Two at Prenton Park, Birkenhead, on Saturday 21 November 2026, with the home side's winner coming in the 90th minute. It ends a short lift for Danny Cowley's side, who had beaten Gillingham 2-0 a week earlier for their first league win since the end of August.

Tranmere had the better of the opening stages and went ahead shortly before the half-hour mark, when Ince, back in Darrell Clarke's starting line-up, picked up a loose ball, drove forward and finished. Colchester were level just before the break as Raggett scored from a Jack Payne cross, and the sides went in at 1-1. Jones then won it for Tranmere in the final minute of normal time.

Colchester went into the game 21st in League Two, three points above the relegation zone, and stay on 15 points. They are back at the JobServe Community Stadium against York City on Saturday 28 November (3pm), go to Grimsby Town on Tuesday 1 December, then host Mansfield Town in the FA Cup second round on Saturday 5 December.

stories.headline: Shrimpers lose five-goal table-top thriller
stories.summary: Tyreece Simpson and debutant Rico Richards struck two minutes apart after the break, but the Shrimpers could not complete the comeback against the runaway leaders.
body: Southend United 2-3 Boreham Wood. The Shrimpers' comeback against the National League leaders fell one goal short in front of 9,985 fans at Roots Hall on Friday night.

The Shrimpers were 3-0 down by the 33rd minute, with a former Southend player among the scorers. Oliver Bainbridge finished inside the near post on 19 minutes and Ben Whitfield converted at the far post on 29, both set up by Regan Booty, before ex-Shrimper Zak Brunt slammed in from close range from Whitfield's pass.

Southend made three changes at half-time, sending on Maxwell McKnight, Tyreece Simpson and Anthony Hartigan for Leon Chambers-Parillon, Omari Patrick and Zavier Massiah-Edwards. Simpson headed in McKnight's cross on 65 minutes, and two minutes later Rico Richards, making his debut after coming on for Oliver Coker just before the hour, fired in off the far post from Promise Omochere's pass.

Roots Hall roared for an equaliser through the remaining 23 minutes and four minutes of added time, but it never came. Southend were shown six yellow cards, to Omochere, Daniel Cox, Ben Goodliffe, Simpson, Hartigan and Darren Oldaker.
Head coach Kieron Dyer was back in the dugout after a one-match touchline ban for a game shown live on DAZN.
Boreham Wood's 15th league win of the season stretched their unbeaten start to 18 matches and moved them 13 points clear at the top of the National League.

body: Luc Benkenstein has left Essex by mutual agreement and will join Durham as part of the deal, the club announced on Thursday 19 November.

The all-rounder arrived at Chelmsford in 2021 and made his debut that season in the One Day Cup, against Durham. He went on to play 80 times for Essex across all formats, and had signed a contract extension that ran until the end of the 2027 season.

His father, former South Africa international Dale Benkenstein, was appointed a batting consultant at Durham in March. Essex thanked Benkenstein for his efforts and commitment and wished him well for the future.

The sisters joined Essex on a sports scholarship in autumn 2025 with Glasgow as their goal. They train at Pipers Vale Gymnastics Club in Ipswich and also compete for the Essex Blades in student competitions, where Emily won gold and Abigail bronze at the BUCS championships in February.

stories.headline: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck, who taught art in Colchester, dies at 85
stories.summary: The artist helped create one of Britain's most iconic television programmes, but before achieving worldwide fame he taught at Colchester School of Art.
body: Peter Fluck, the artist and caricaturist who co-created the satirical television series Spitting Image, has died aged 85.
Fluck, who taught art at Colchester School of Art during the 1970s, died at his home in Cornwall in the early hours of Saturday, November 21, following a recent illness, his family said.

He became one of the most influential figures in British television satire through Spitting Image, the ITV programme which used grotesque puppet caricatures to mock politicians, celebrities, royalty and other prominent figures.
But before the show made him a household name, Fluck spent part of his career teaching aspiring artists in Colchester.
## From art teacher to television satire
Born in Cambridge in 1941, Fluck studied at Cambridge School of Art, where he met fellow artist Roger Law.
The pair went on to establish a creative partnership, initially working as freelance illustrators and caricaturists before developing the idea that would transform their careers.
Spitting Image first aired in 1984, bringing their exaggerated puppet creations to television screens across Britain.

The programme became famous for its uncompromising portrayal of the country's political establishment, with Margaret Thatcher, John Major, members of the Royal Family and international figures among its regular targets.
At its peak, the series attracted audiences of around 15 million viewers and became one of the defining television programmes of the 1980s and 1990s.
It ran for 18 series before ending in 1996.
## A lasting legacy
Fluck and Law's creations helped redefine political satire, combining caricature, puppetry and comedy to produce some of the most recognisable television characters of their era.
The programme won numerous awards, including two Emmy Awards, and its influence extended beyond television into music, popular culture and political commentary.
After Spitting Image ended, Fluck continued his artistic career, turning his attention to sculpture and moving installations from his studio in Cornwall.
His family described him as a private man who avoided fame and attention.
In a statement, they said: "The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining.
"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image."
They added that his creative life continued for many years after the programme from his studio in Cornwall.
His death marks the loss of one of the artists behind a television phenomenon which remains synonymous with British satire.

body: Gareth Stafford Bull, Brentwood School's fencing coach from about 1982 until he was sacked in 1997, probably abused a number of boys at the school, an independent review commissioned by its governors has found. The review also says the school let down former pupils who came forward in the years after his death.

When one of them raised concerns with the school in 2008, the headmaster of the day replied that he had seen no evidence, even though the school's own files recorded that police had found prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997.

Bull was himself a Brentwood pupil before he returned as its fencing instructor. Published results show he fenced for the school as a boy, finishing third in the boys' senior sabre at the 1974 Public Schools' Fencing Championships. The review says he also coached the England under-20 fencing team, and that former pupils told it he abused other boys while he was still a pupil and went on doing so throughout his time as a coach.

He was suspended and then sacked for gross misconduct in April 1997, after police told the school that pupils had raised concerns about him. He died in May 1997 before the police investigation could go further, so he never faced trial. The review's findings about him are made on the balance of probability, the standard used in civil cases, rather than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
## Who wrote the review

The findings come from the "Review into the abuse by David Pickthall of pupils and former pupils of Brentwood School", a 59-page report commissioned by the school's governing body and published on the school's website this month. It was led by two independent members. Louisa Spicer, who chaired it, is a former solicitor with more than 20 years' experience in employment law and human resources. Jane Foster (Sarre) is an independent safeguarding adviser, consultant and trainer who has led school safeguarding audits. They were supported by three governors who had no part in managing Pickthall: Bob McLintock, John Griffith-Jones and the Venerable Chris Burke. The Seax has read the full report.

The governors commissioned the review on 23 November 2024, days after Pickthall, the school's former director of music, was jailed. He admitted 29 offences against 19 male victims between 1979 and 2021, most of them his former pupils, and was sentenced to 12 years with a further four on extended licence. He was asked to take part in the review but declined. It began work in March 2025, and as well as Pickthall's abuse, its remit covered other historical allegations about former members of the school community. That is where the findings about the fencing coach appear.
The reviewers say the school kept virtually no records for the 1980s and 1990s, so they relied heavily on court transcripts and on accounts from former pupils and staff.
## What happened in 1997

The details of Bull's appointment are not in his personnel file, which is thin. Its first document is a complaint from the head of Brentwood Prep in May 1989 that he was unreliable and missed lessons. In 1990 the headmaster gave him a first written warning over his absences and an unpaid accommodation bill of £1,000, while praising his "tremendous success" as a coach and telling him the school was in his debt.

In April 1997 the headmaster wrote to the parents of pupils involved in fencing to tell them Bull had been suspended. A note on his file records that a small group of boys had come forward to a member of staff. The concerns included encouraging boys to shower after competitions and joining them. Governing body minutes from 21 April record that police enquiries, prompted by an anonymous call, had found prima facie evidence of indecent behaviour involving members of the school fencing team, particularly on trips away. By then Bull was missing from home, and the headmaster judged the evidence against him to be incontrovertible. He was dismissed the next day.

The headmaster gave police a list of pupils who had been taught by Bull, and officers interviewed them at the school. On 27 April more pupils who had contact with him were seen one by one in the headmaster's office. The brief notes kept from those meetings confirm that a number of pupils said Bull had suggested they shower with him. Bull died on 5 May 1997, and his death and the police investigation were reported in the national press.
## What former pupils told the review

One former pupil told the review that Bull abused boys on what he called "an industrial scale", including intimate massages, coming into boys' rooms on residential trips, sexualised conversation and invasive questions about their sexuality. Bull travelled alone with pupils and sometimes shared rooms with them. They said he also befriended parents, visiting their homes and having dinner with them. One described him as effectively part of the staff although he was not a full-time employee, coming and going as he pleased, and said pupils talked about him only on a surface level. Contributors said staff must have heard rumours. The review says the full extent of his offending is not known and that more victim-survivors may come forward.
## How the school handled later complaints

Former pupils contacted the school about Bull in 2008, 2017 and 2024. In 2008 a former fencer told the headmaster of the time, who had not been at the school while Bull worked there, that many of his contemporaries had been abused and had suffered mental and physical breakdowns, and asked what support the school had offered. The review says the headmaster's reply contradicts the evidence in Bull's own personnel file and in governing body minutes, and it found no sign of any follow-up.

In 2017 another former pupil emailed the chairman of governors to say Bull had abused him when they were both pupils, and was told to go to the police. The review has not seen the reply and does not know who sent it. It found no record that the email was passed to the headmaster, the safeguarding lead or the police, which it says was by then a failure to meet statutory guidance, and it describes the response to him as dismissive. The same man told the review that another former member of staff had set up a situation in which he felt obliged to shower with Bull. In 2024 a third former pupil told the school it had never held itself accountable for the number of pupils Bull abused.

The review concludes that police held prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997 and that, on the balance of probability, a number of pupils were harmed by him both when he was a pupil and while he was a coach at the school. It found no evidence that the school pursued the matter after his death or offered support to anyone affected, and that its later responses to former pupils were inadequate and lacked empathy. It says further investigation now is unlikely to change those findings.
## Pickthall, and the school's culture

The review found no evidence that Pickthall and Bull worked together, but says the prestige both men brought, as a renowned musician and a fencing coach, may have made school leaders reluctant to believe concerns about them. Former pupils described Pickthall as godlike and bigger than the school, and one described the school of the mid-1980s to mid-1990s as having a culture of fear. Pupils told the review they did not report abuse because they feared not being believed or harming their chances in music. On Pickthall, the review found anonymous allegations in 2007, 2009 and 2014 were not properly investigated, and a misplaced personnel file meant earlier warnings were not seen.

The review also heard what it called credible accounts of abuse by other staff in the 1960s and 1970s, including harsh physical punishment, and of abuse by pupils. It says the staff named in those accounts have died or cannot be traced.
## What the school says

In a foreword, the chairman of governors, Lord Black of Brentwood, who was a pupil at the school in the 1970s and early 1980s, offers a "deep, sincere and unreserved apology" to everyone abused in the school's past. He says the governors have accepted the report and all its recommendations, and that the school has learned the lessons. Nobody, he writes, will ever again hide behind the idea that it could not happen there, because it did.

Lord Black says safeguarding is now the first item of business whenever governors meet, and that the school has changed out of all recognition since Pickthall left in 2014. He points to inspections by the Independent Schools Inspectorate in 2019, 2022 and 2025, and to two independent safeguarding reviews the school commissioned in light of Pickthall's crimes, in 2022 and 2025. The review itself agrees that safeguarding at the school today is strong, well resourced and led from the top, and that pupils describe the school as happy and safe.

On its website, the school lists 17 designated safeguarding leads and deputies. It says every senior school pupil carries a card with the names of people they can talk to and the numbers of outside organisations, and that pupils can report a concern through an online platform called The Student Voice.
## What happens next

The review makes recommendations that the school has accepted. They include publicly acknowledging the harm done by Pickthall, Bull, other adults and pupils, and accepting that the school failed to detect abuse during the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s; sharing the report with the Essex Safeguarding Children Board; sharing the findings about Bull with British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee; training staff and governors in how sex offenders groom children; and checking that no other complaints about current or former staff have been misfiled.

British Fencing said on Friday 20 November that it would commission its own independent safeguarding review into the role, if any, of the sport's governing body and its predecessor, the Amateur Fencing Association. The former pupil who wrote to the school in 2017 has asked, in his evidence to the review, whether British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee were told about Bull in 1997.

Outside the school, Bull coached at Wickford Fencing Club from 1979 to 1987, according to the club's history page, which lists him among its previous coaches. The review makes no findings about his time at the Wickford club.
## About Brentwood School

Brentwood School was founded in 1557 by Sir Antony Browne, a lawyer who later became one of England's most senior judges, and received its licence from Queen Mary on 5 July 1558. Its Tudor schoolroom, Old Big School, was built in 1568.

Today it is a private, fee-paying school and a registered charity, with more than 1,800 boys and girls aged 3 to 18 and boarding for older pupils. Boys and girls are taught together in the prep school and sixth form, but in separate classes from 11 to 16, an approach the school calls the Diamond Model.

Fees for 2026/27 are £30,204 a year for day pupils from Year 7 to the sixth form, including VAT, which has been charged on private school fees since January 2025. Full boarding costs £58,464 a year. Fees for younger pupils run from £16,500 a year for three-year-olds to £23,076 in Years 3 to 6. The school's charity had an income of £44.9 million in the year to August 2024, according to the Charity Commission.

Except where stated, everything in this story comes from the review. The 1974 result comes from published championship results, his Wickford coaching from the club's own website, details of the school's safeguarding team from its website, and British Fencing's plans from its statement on Friday. The school's history, fees and size come from its own website, the Independent Schools Council and the Independent Schools Yearbook, and its income from the Charity Commission register.
## Where to get help

Brentwood School says victim-survivors can contact the headmaster or the chairman of governors in confidence. The review lists organisations that support adults abused in childhood: NAPAC on 0808 801 0331, Stop It Now on 0808 1000 900, SERICC on 01375 380609 and CARA Essex on 01206 769795. British Fencing has a form for reporting a safeguarding concern on its website. Samaritans is available any time on 116 123.

stories.headline: Colchester leaders rule out Leisure World rebuild ahead of cabinet vote
stories.summary: Upgrading the ageing Cowdray Avenue centre is the only practical way to protect public swimming in the city, Colchester City Council says.
body: The council looked at knocking down Leisure World and building a new centre, but judged that the cost and the years it would take ruled that out for now, it said on 16 November. Instead, council leaders want a programme of work on the existing site covering essential building infrastructure, customer facilities and the systems that keep the centre running.

The plans were examined by the council's Scrutiny Committee on 11 November and go to the Cabinet for a final decision on Wednesday 2 December. The council says fuller details and a timetable for the work will follow if they are approved.

Council leader Paul Dundas, Conservative councillor for Tiptree, said that like many ageing public buildings, the site "now requires major investment". A brand-new centre would have been the ideal answer, he said, but it was not viable at this stage. He said it would not be "remotely acceptable" for a city of more than 200,000 people to have no public swimming, and called the plan the biggest investment in Leisure World for a generation.

The council has not yet said what the programme will cost. Its 2026/27 budget, agreed in February, set aside £8 million to be invested in Leisure World. After the scrutiny meeting, Mr Dundas told the Daily Gazette the centre would have faced permanent closure within months without the investment.

The work would follow the £1.4 million refurbishment of the Leisure Pool, which closed at the end of September and is due to reopen in early 2027. That project covers relining the pool, new changing areas, work on the outdoor flumes, better ventilation, a new splash pad and upgraded water features. The rest of Leisure World has stayed open, though its main pool [shut for cleaning after an incident](/story/colchester-leisure-world-swimming-pool-closed-incident/) on Friday 20 November.

The decision comes as Essex councils are reorganised. Colchester has said that during 2026/27 it expects to share any substantial financial decisions with the other councils that will form its new unitary authority.

stories.headline: Former Ravens store in Southend could become 17-room shared house
stories.summary: The developer wants to drop a students-only rule on rooms above the old Clifftown Road store, opposite Southend Central station.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council gave permission for 17 student rooms on the first, second and third floors of 6-7 Clifftown Road on 28 November 2025, and those floors have since been converted, Your Southend reports. A new application from McNamara, Brook and Mac Property Developments Ltd, registered on 16 November 2026, asks for the same 17 rooms to become a house in multiple occupation (HMO) that anyone can rent.

Days after the 2025 approval, on 2 December, the University of Essex announced it would close its Southend campus. It shut at the end of August 2026, with courses moving to Colchester. Your Southend says it is not known whether the closure led to the new plan.
## What is a shared house, or HMO?

Under the Housing Act 2004, an HMO is a home rented by at least three people who are not one family and who share a kitchen, bathroom or toilet. Each tenant normally rents their own room and shares the rest. The council's guidance counts a family, or a couple, as one household.

When five or more people from two or more households share, the HMO needs a licence from the council, and running one without a licence is a criminal offence. Shared houses for more than six people also fall outside the usual planning categories for homes, so they need full planning permission.
## What happens next

The council normally writes to neighbours and puts up a site notice, and anyone can comment on the plans on its planning website using reference 26/01422/FUL. Planning officers usually decide applications like this themselves, but a councillor can ask for one to go to the council's Development Control Committee, as happened with a 15-bed HMO in Cobham Road, Westcliff, in 2023.
## What the council will look at

Southend's planning rules set minimum bedroom sizes in shared homes of 6.5 square metres for one person and 10.2 square metres for two, require shared living space, and steer this kind of housing towards the city centre, where the building stands. Officers also weigh noise and privacy for neighbours, bin storage, cycle parking and transport. In the Cobham Road report, officers proposed conditions including a cap on the number of residents and a secure cycle space for every room.

The council can approve the plans, approve them with conditions or refuse them. If they are refused, the developer can appeal to the Planning Inspectorate. Until a decision is made, the existing permission means the rooms can only be let to students.
## If the plans are approved

If permission is granted, the landlord would still need an HMO licence before the rooms are let to five or more people. Licences cover fire safety, overcrowding, repairs and the kitchens and bathrooms tenants share, and the council says its private sector housing officers visit every HMO in the city. Failing to apply for a licence can bring a penalty of up to £30,000, and the council can take over the running of a property that should be licensed but is not.
## The rest of the building

The ground-floor shop and basement are not part of the plan. They are being marketed separately to businesses at £54,000 a year, Your Southend reports. Ravens, a family-run department store best known for its menswear, closed in 2017.

stories.headline: Brentwood raid nets 616kg of raw tobacco in illegal cigarette crackdown
stories.summary: The unit was one of several sites searched as HMRC shut down a Lincolnshire factory able to make 200,000 cigarettes a day.
body: Officers seized 616kg of raw tobacco from an industrial unit in the Brentwood area during a nationwide HM Revenue and Customs operation against illegal cigarette production, HMRC has revealed.

The raids on 10 November centred on an industrial site in Bourne, Lincolnshire, where HMRC says it found a fully working cigarette factory. Officers seized 808,840 cigarettes and about 4.8 tonnes of tobacco there, along with machinery for cutting and drying tobacco and for making and packing cigarettes. HMRC's first assessment is that the plant could produce more than 200,000 cigarettes a day.

About 200 officers carried out 12 search warrants at homes and industrial premises across England. Besides the Brentwood unit, they searched industrial premises in Grantham, Kirkby-in-Ashfield and Northampton. From homes in Willenhall, Greenwich and Newham they took £645,000 in cash and four gold bars worth about £213,500. In all, more than 1.4 million cigarettes and about 5.5 tonnes of tobacco were seized, carrying an estimated £4.5m in duty.

Twenty-one people were arrested on suspicion of offences linked to the fraudulent evasion of excise duty. All have been released pending further enquiries. HMRC has not said where in the Brentwood area the unit is. The operation was led by HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, supported by police, the East Midlands Special Operations Unit and the Home Office.

Raw tobacco is the unprocessed leaf that cigarettes are made from. Since April 2017 anyone in the UK who holds, moves or uses it has needed HMRC's approval under the Raw Tobacco Approval Scheme, which was brought in to stop leaf being diverted into illegal cigarette making.

Margaret Mousley, deputy director of HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, said: "This was a major operation which dismantled a huge cigarette factory, disrupting the organised criminality that sits behind it. Our investigation into that criminality is ongoing." HMRC is asking anyone with information about the illegal manufacture or sale of tobacco to report it online.

stories.headline: Maldon Salt labelling questions passed to Essex Trading Standards
stories.summary: Maldon District Council says it has no concerns about Maldon Salt's sites, the Maldon Standard reports, after an Observer investigation found the firm mixes German rock salt into its sea salt.

stories.newAngle: Maldon District Council has now said it has no concerns about the firm's sites, and Essex Trading Standards will deal with labelling questions.
body: Labelling is not a matter for the district council. In Essex it falls to the county council's trading standards service, which has looked at how Maldon Salt is made before, as [our story last Sunday on the Observer's findings](/story/maldon-salt-german-rock-salt-sea-salt-observer/) set out.
## What trading standards found in 2019

Trading standards officers visited the firm's works at Longwick Farm, near Goldhanger, with the Food Standards Agency on 6 November 2019 and took samples. After advice from a public analyst, the FSA and Defra, they decided no further action was needed. Maldon Salt says the FSA and trading standards are satisfied with how its product is described and know exactly how the rock salt is used.

A county council trading standards spokesperson told the Observer there were no specific legal rules for deciding whether a product can accurately be described as sea salt. The UK has no legal definition of sea salt, and The Grocer, the food industry's trade magazine, says that means Maldon is doing nothing wrong under current UK labelling law.
## A stricter rule in Canada

Other countries draw the line more clearly. Canada's food inspection agency says sea salt means salt processed from an existing sea, and salt from a mine cannot be labelled that way. In Canada, Maldon's packs are labelled Maldon Salt and list the ingredient as salt flakes. The Observer reported that the firm had not commented on the change.
## What the Observer found

As [The Seax reported last Sunday](/story/maldon-salt-german-rock-salt-sea-salt-observer/), an Observer investigation found that Maldon Salt mixes rock salt mined in Germany by K+S into the seawater it draws from the Blackwater estuary, and estimated that about 50 tonnes arrive each week. The paper reported that the firm bought its rock salt from Cheshire until about 2020 and has mostly bought it from Germany since.

Maldon Salt does not dispute that some of the added rock salt ends up in the finished flakes. It says rock salt is ancient sea salt from prehistoric seas, that its "100% sea salt flakes" label is accurate, that it has never hidden its salt-on-salt method, and that its products comply with food and labelling law in every market where they are sold.
## The planning history

Deliveries of salt to Longwick Farm have a long planning history. The Observer reported that the 2006 permission for the works covered salt made from Blackwater water, that a condition added in 2011 banned salt being delivered to the site for making or selling salt, and that the firm applied to lift it the following year, was refused by the council and won on appeal. Neighbours have questioned the deliveries since they first filmed them in 2010.
Maldon Salt has made salt in the town for 144 years and is a major local employer. No UK regulator has taken action against it over the way its salt is made or labelled.

stories.headline: One of Essex Police's first female detective sergeants retires after 48 years
stories.summary: Deirdre Nowell joined the force in 1978, when a woman officer's uniform came with a handbag and an allowance for tights.
body: She followed her older brother, Kevin, into Essex Police. The force describes her as a self-confessed maverick with a sharp sense of humour and a dedication to high standards, and calls her retirement the end of an era.

Her early years were eventful. One of her first jobs for CID involved having to drink in a student bar, and in her first year she was sent flying through the window of a shop in Colchester after being hit by a car.

A newspaper cutting from her recruit days, shared by the force, shows her in the front row of a new intake under the headline "Almost half recruit squad are women". It names her as the most successful recruit at training school and says she was posted to Colchester.

Later in her career she became an innovator. Her work on HOLMES, the computer system police use to manage information during major investigations, and on the National Police Chiefs' Council's Casualty Bureau saw her ideas adopted across the country.
She is a former winner of the force's Liam Brigginshaw Award for outstanding commitment, which she received in 2024.
Essex Police shared the news of her retirement on its Facebook page on Saturday morning, and says more about her career is on its website.
points: Hit by a car and thrown through a Colchester shop window in her first year

stories.headline: Dengie solar farm: wider public consultation planned for early 2027
stories.summary: Residents across the Dengie Peninsula will get a fuller say on Low Carbon's seven-site, 4,200-acre plan before the firm applies to the government for consent.
body: The sites run from near the closed Bradwell nuclear power station to Burnham-on-Crouch, passing Tillingham and Southminster. Together they cover 1,700 hectares, about the size of 2,400 football pitches, and Low Carbon describes the scheme as one of the biggest solar farms in the UK. Simon Morgan, the Conservative leader of Maldon District Council, estimates it would take up almost a third of the land on the peninsula.
Essex County Council's map of the area affected covers Bradwell Waterside and Mill End, and land around the edges of Southminster, Asheldham, Burnham and Tillingham.
## What is planned

The project, called Dengie Peninsula Energy Park, would combine solar panels with battery storage and an on-site substation. Low Carbon says it could generate up to 1GW, or 1,000 megawatts, enough to meet the yearly electricity needs of about 250,000 homes, and would avoid up to 265,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

The power would be carried to the National Grid's substation at Rayleigh along the existing overhead line from Bradwell, using pylons that once served the nuclear power station. Low Carbon already has a grid connection offer there. It is also keeping open a second option at the former Bradwell substation, although it has no offer for that yet.

The company says it chose the Dengie for its sunshine, its large flat fields and the grid links left behind by the power station. The scheme is being developed by Dengie Peninsula Energy Park Limited, part of Low Carbon, a renewable energy company founded in 2011.
## Who decides

Because it would generate more than 100 megawatts, the scheme counts as a nationally significant infrastructure project and needs a development consent order. The Planning Inspectorate would examine any application, and the Energy Secretary, not Maldon District Council, would make the final decision. The council says it will still give planning and technical advice and speak up for local communities, working with Essex County Council.
## What happens next

The plans are at an early stage. Low Carbon has asked the Planning Inspectorate to agree which environmental studies it must carry out, and Maldon District Council has until Tuesday 24 November to send its comments. The studies would look at the landscape and views, wildlife and habitats, the loss of farmland, construction traffic, new power lines, noise, effects on aircraft and glare from the panels. The council stresses this is not a vote on whether the park should go ahead.

Low Carbon plans a wider public consultation in early 2027 and aims to submit its application to the Planning Inspectorate by the end of that year. Essex County Council expects it in October 2027. If it is approved, the company's project website says building would start in 2030, the park would be fully running in early 2034, and it would have a working life of about 40 years.
## The concerns

James Taylor, chairman of the Dengie Climate Action Partnership, told BBC News the scale had "slightly knocked people sideways", and said he was torn between backing renewable energy and worrying about wildlife. Roger Morland, chairman of Burnham Against Non-Sustainable Development, pointed to the area's international importance for wildlife and its protection as a Site of Special Scientific Interest.

Campaigners fear harm to a key bird migration route and to country roads while the park is built. Low Carbon says extensive bird surveys are under way, some building materials could arrive by boat, and reusing the old grid lines means less new infrastructure. Ed Perrin, its development director, argues that schemes on this scale are needed to meet the country's targets for cutting carbon.
## Have your say

Low Carbon says it is still at an early stage and plans a wider public consultation in early 2027. Maldon District Council says residents will get another chance to comment then, before any application is made, and that its current comments on the environmental studies do not give permission to build.

The project team can be contacted on 0800 047 8766, by email at info@dengiepeninsulaenergypark.co.uk or through the feedback form on the project website. Documents submitted so far, including the environmental scoping report, are on the Planning Inspectorate's project pages.

stories.headline: Two taken to hospital after A282 crash shuts QEII Bridge for hours
stories.summary: Both were taken by road to the Royal London Hospital, and more closures are planned at the Dartford Crossing tonight and on Saturday.
body: A crash on the clockwise A282 in Thurrock shut the QEII Bridge at the Dartford Crossing for around three hours on Friday 20 November, and two people were taken to hospital, Brentwood Live reported.

The East of England Ambulance Service said it was called at 10.30am to a collision on the M25 near junction 31, on the approach to the bridge. It sent two ambulances, an ambulance officer, a rapid response vehicle and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance, and two patients were taken by road to the Royal London Hospital.

Firefighters freed the two people, who were trapped in their vehicles, and handed them to paramedics, the Echo reported. Essex Police said four vehicles were involved; the Echo reported that they included two lorries and a car, and that the air ambulance landed on a grass verge near junction 30.

Queues built up across south Essex. At about 12.15pm, National Highways' overhead signs showed the M25 closed at junction 30 and delays of more than an hour between junctions 29 and 1A. By the afternoon, the AA was reporting delays of about 20 minutes on the bridge and about 29 minutes for traffic heading to junction 30 from junction 27, according to Brentwood Live.

More closures are planned at the crossing. The west tunnel, which carries northbound traffic, is due to close from 9pm tonight until 5.30am on Saturday, according to National Highways' roadworks data. National Highways has also confirmed the QEII Bridge will close from 10.30pm on Saturday until 5.30am on Sunday, London Now reported.
The condition of the two people taken to hospital has not been released. This story will be updated.

body: Police in Essex logged 2,042 reports of anti-social behaviour in September 2026, up from 1,162 in September 2025, according to the street-level records published on police.uk. Recorded crime rose more slowly, to 12,530 from 11,563. Both figures were lower than in August.
Some of the rise in anti-social behaviour may come from changes in how police record it, rather than from more incidents. The figures do not show how much.

Violence and sexual offences remain by far the largest category of crime. Police recorded 5,800 of them in September, up 15% from 5,045 a year earlier, and they made up almost half of all recorded crime in the county.
Thefts rose too. Shoplifting went up 22% to 1,265 offences, theft from the person rose by half to 126, and other theft climbed 20% to 1,008.

Most other types of crime fell. Robbery dropped 19%, from 132 to 107, and bicycle theft fell 12% to 94. Criminal damage and arson went down 8% to 981, vehicle crime 6% to 851 and burglary 3% to 376. Drug offences, public order offences and possession of weapons were also slightly lower.

Anti-social behaviour reports rose in 50 of Essex Police's 56 neighbourhood areas. Basildon had the most, with 151 reports against 76 a year earlier, followed by Colchester Town West with 112 and Southend Central with 110.

Among the 10 areas with the most reports, three more than doubled their totals: Chelmsford Town, from 38 to 86; Chafford Hundred and Grays, from 51 to 107; and Colchester Town East, from 36 to 75. Only one of the 10, Aveley and Ockendon, saw a fall, from 57 to 54.

Taking crime and anti-social behaviour together, records rose in 45 neighbourhoods and fell in 11. Clacton had the biggest rise, with 151 more records than a year earlier, followed by Westcliff (129 more), Basildon (118 more) and Chelmsford South (115 more). In Westcliff, shoplifting nearly trebled.
The biggest falls were in Wakering, with 21 fewer records, Thundersley, with 19 fewer, and Canvey, with 18 fewer.

Police.uk's anti-social behaviour category covers personal, environmental and nuisance anti-social behaviour. It is recorded separately from crime and is not part of the official recorded crime statistics.
Anti-social behaviour and crimes that are not emergencies can be reported to Essex Police online at essex.police.uk or by calling 101. Call 999 if a crime is happening now or someone is in danger.

Police.uk places each record at an approximate location rather than an exact address. The Seax counted every record inside the boundaries of the 56 neighbourhood areas. A few records sit exactly on the line between two neighbourhoods and appear in both neighbourhoods' figures, but each is counted once in the county totals. A further 216 crimes in September had no location and are not included. Totals may differ slightly from Essex Police's own figures.
The figures cover the whole Essex Police area, including Southend and Thurrock, and can be checked street by street on police.uk.

body: NHS Essex is looking for new software to handle online consultations at the 204 GP surgeries it covers, and has asked suppliers to show what their systems can do before it decides what to buy.

The integrated care board, which plans and pays for NHS services for about 1.9 million people in Essex, wants a contract lasting two years, PublicTechnology reported on Friday 20 November. The notice does not say how much it is worth.

Online consultations let patients contact their surgery through its website, to describe a problem or ask for advice, and the request goes straight to the practice. At the moment, Essex surgeries use a range of different systems, chosen to suit local needs, the notice says.

The board says practices with similar needs could be grouped together when it buys the new service, so not every surgery would necessarily end up with the same system. Nothing has been decided yet: not what it needs, how it will buy it or which company will win.

This first step is what the Procurement Act 2023 calls preliminary market engagement. Suppliers can demonstrate their systems at an online event on 9 December, where GP practices and the board can ask questions, and must register by 3 December. Taking part gives a company no advantage when the contract is later put out to tender, the notice says.

The plans come weeks after a problem with a website provider left some GP practice websites and online consultation services in north east Essex unavailable. NHS Essex said on 28 October that practices remained open, and pointed patients to the NHS App, Pharmacy First, phoning or emailing their practice, NHS 111, and 999 in a life-threatening emergency.
Any change to the systems patients use would not come before spring 2027, when the new contract is due to begin.

body: Jayne Mason's mother had a red, painful eye and was thinking about going to A&E, NHS Essex said on Friday 20 November. Her usual optician had no appointment, so Ms Mason found a practice in Pitsea taking part in the Minor Eye Conditions Service. After a short phone assessment her mother was seen within 30 minutes and told nothing was seriously wrong.

The free service runs at participating opticians across Essex, with no GP referral needed. It covers new problems such as red or sore eyes, dry or gritty eyes, swelling, watery eyes, new flashes or floaters, eye pain, ingrowing eyelashes and grit in the eye. In a survey of 641 patients in mid and south Essex between April and June 2026, 96% said they would recommend it, and 20% said they would otherwise have gone to A&E.

Dr Boye Tayo, clinical lead for eye care at NHS Essex, said the board wants more people to know the service exists. Patients should call a participating practice first rather than turn up. NHS Essex says anyone who suddenly loses sight, has severe eye pain, a serious eye injury or a strong chemical in the eye should go to A&E or call 999.

stories.summary: Clubs and groups across the Tendring district can bid for money for projects that get people active, eating well or looking after their mental health.
body: Sports clubs and community groups in the Tendring district have until Sunday 3 January 2027 to apply, Tendring District Council said on Friday 20 November. Bids can cover active travel, club development and disability sport, sport for young children and after school, food and nutrition for families, or mental health.

The council says more than £110,000 is on offer in all. The money comes from its sports strategy budget and public health funding, with a share from the Love Clacton Town Board, part of the government's Pride in Place scheme. Councillor Mick Barry, cabinet member for sport and leisure, said 'just a little bit of cash can really kick-start something fantastic'. Councillor Gina Placey, cabinet member for partnerships, said being active helps mental health and can ease loneliness.

Groups can find out how to apply at free Sports Forum evenings. They are at the Columbine Centre in Walton-on-the-Naze on Thursday 26 November at 6pm, Mistley Parish Hall on Tuesday 1 December at 6.15pm, Dovercourt Bay Lifestyles Leisure Centre on Friday 4 December at 6pm and Brightlingsea Parish Hall on Monday 7 December at 6pm. stories.summary: A High Street restaurant has the lowest rating, zero, and two other city centre businesses are rated one after inspections in October, an analysis of Food Standards Agency data by The Seax shows.
body: Bees Indian Restaurant & Bar at 105 High Street, Colchester, is rated 0, which the Food Standards Agency describes as urgent improvement necessary, after an inspection on 14 October 2026. King of Spice, a takeaway at 59 East Street, is rated 1, meaning major improvement necessary, after an inspection on 6 October. Vinny's Restaurant at 1 Headgate is also rated 1 after a visit on 8 October.

The ratings are those shown on the Food Standards Agency's website on 20 November and reflect what Colchester City Council inspectors found on those dates. Each business can appeal, ask for a re-inspection once it has made improvements, or publish its own reply on the ratings website. The published data gives scores only, not the inspectors' notes, so it does not show what the problems were.

Across Colchester low ratings are rare. Of 1,413 rated premises in the city council's area, 0.9% have a rating of 0, 1 or 2 and 90.7% have the top rating of 5. In Rochford and Tendring the share of low ratings is above 4%, although councils inspect at different rates, so the figures are a guide rather than a league table. Every rating can be checked at ratings.food.gov.uk.

The redeveloped area now houses an urgent treatment centre, community paediatrics, children's therapies and the musculoskeletal therapy service. NHS England and NHS Property Services also helped pay for the work. Paul Scott, chief executive of the hospital trust, welcomed the councillors on the visit.

The council's money came from Government-backed Community Regeneration Partnership funding, which also pays for projects in Clacton and Jaywick Sands. stories.summary: Essex County Fire and Rescue Service believes a thrown-away battery started the Little Thurrock scrapyard fire. About 20 firefighters had it out by 8.50pm on 19 November.
body: About 80 tonnes of scrap metal was burning when crews reached the yard off Rectory Road, Little Thurrock, at 6.08pm on Thursday 19 November. After putting it out, firefighters worked with site staff to break up the scrap and check for hotspots. They left at 9.30pm.

Station Manager Rick Williams said batteries can catch fire if they are damaged or crushed. He asked people to take used batteries to a recycling centre or collection point, and never to put them in a skip or with general rubbish.

Smoke from the fire drifted across Grays during the evening, and neighbours were told to keep their windows shut. The yard is on the Globe Industrial Estate, close to homes, where six fire crews fought a building fire in June 2022.

body: Essex Police released the little boy's name and his family's tribute on Wednesday 18 November, five weeks after officers were called to an address in Eagle Way, Shoeburyness. Ambulance crews had raised concerns for a child's welfare there just before 8am on Monday 12 October, and detectives opened an investigation after Blake died.

"My precious little boy was loved more than words could ever explain," his family said. They said they longed for one more cuddle with him, and thanked everyone who has shown them kindness and support.

A 24-year-old man from Rayleigh and a 26-year-old woman from Shoeburyness were arrested as part of the investigation into Blake's death. Both are on conditional bail while enquiries continue, Essex Police said, and the family have asked for privacy while the investigation takes its course.

stories.headline: Nearly 100 Colchester households stuck in B&Bs as housing demand climbs
stories.summary: Officers warn the city's homelessness budget will be heavily overspent this year as more families are placed in temporary homes.
points: The city is above its own target for households in temporary accommodation

Cabinet takes the council's half-year report on 2 December
body: Colchester had 588 households in temporary accommodation at the end of September, 98 of them in bed and breakfasts, according to the council's latest quarterly housing report, which goes before councillors shortly. The total was 550 three months earlier and 472 in mid-November last year, a rise of almost a quarter, the Daily Gazette reports. It puts the city at seven households in temporary accommodation for every 1,000, above the council's own target of six.

The council's half-year performance report, discussed by its scrutiny panel on 11 November and due before cabinet on 2 December, says 616 households facing homelessness were being supported by 31 October. Council leader Paul Dundas said demand for housing "remains extremely high". The pressure has built quickly: the council's own figures showed 326 households in temporary accommodation in March 2024 and 449 a year later, while Colchester Borough Homes, which runs the city's homelessness service, assessed 1,563 new homelessness cases in 2024/25.

The council has turned former private student flats into temporary homes, a scheme that won a bronze award at the Local Government Chronicle awards in June, and plans to buy 65 homes during 2026/27 to cut its reliance on costly temporary accommodation. It has previously said it uses B&Bs only when it is urgent and for short periods. Nationally, the government has committed to ending the unlawful use of B&Bs for families, and a new Colchester homelessness and rough sleeping strategy for 2026 to 2031 aims to step in before households reach crisis point.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring plans to backdate council tax support for working-age claimants
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council wants to extend a rule that now helps only pension-age claimants. Other council tax discounts and premiums in the district stay the same in 2027/28.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet agreed on Friday 13 November 2026 to consult on a change to its Local Council Tax Support scheme for 2027/28. The change would let working-age claimants have their claims backdated by up to 3 months. The council must first consult the major preceptors, the other public bodies that set a share of the council tax bill.

The report to the cabinet says the scheme already lets pension-age claimants backdate claims by 3 months. It says a few recent working-age cases would have benefited from the same help where there was good cause, such as clear proof they were eligible before they applied. The rest of the scheme stays as it is, including a maximum discount of 80% for working-age claimants.

A draft scheme goes back to the cabinet on Friday 11 December 2026. The Resources and Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee will look at it before Full Council decides in January 2027. The cabinet also recommended keeping the 100% council tax premium on second homes and the current premiums on long-term empty homes.

The cabinet also noted an updated financial forecast running to 2029/30. The council is planning for four years in case it still exists beyond April 2028. The cabinet asked the Resources and Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee for its views.

The report recommends a new 25-year lease for the foreshore next to Downs Recreation Ground and another for the foreshore next to Downs Road Boatyard. Both leases would then end in 2051.

The tenant has leased the foreshore by Downs Recreation Ground since 1993 and the boatyard foreshore since 2008. The report says the council must grant a new lease on broadly similar terms unless it has legal grounds to refuse.

The report warns that if councillors say no, the tenant could go to court. A judge would then likely set the rent and terms. The report says the renewals will not affect the council's finances, and council staff will do the legal work.

councilwatch.headline: Basildon Council heads for £3.8m overspend as homelessness costs rise
councilwatch.summary: Repairs and damp and mould work also leave Basildon's council housing account forecast to finish £3.2m over budget in 2026/27, according to a report for the council's Cabinet.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Cabinet will be asked on Thursday 26 November 2026 to note that its General Fund, which pays for most day-to-day services, is forecast to end the year £3.8 million over budget. The forecast, based on spending to the end of September, has grown by £400,000 since the first quarter of the year.

The report blames the cost of the temporary accommodation the council must provide for homeless households, and in particular a shortage of alternatives to expensive nightly paid accommodation. Capital financing, staffing and the risk that planned savings are not delivered add to the pressure, partly offset by extra planning income. On the Housing Revenue Account, which covers council homes, the position has improved by £1.3 million since the first quarter, with the report pointing to rising repair costs, damp and mould cases and the cost of meeting a Regulatory Notice from the Regulator of Social Housing.

The report says any pressures that cannot be managed by the end of the financial year will have to be met from the council's revenue reserves. Services must now set out the actions they are taking each month under a formal recovery plan process, which officers say is showing early signs of working. The revenue figures went to the Finance, Procurement and Efficiency Scrutiny Committee on 16 November 2026 and will feed into setting future budgets.

councilwatch.summary: Community groups wanting to take over a Maldon District Council building or plot would have to show public benefit, local support and sound finances under the draft policy.
body: Maldon District Council's Strategy and Resources Committee will consider an Asset Disposal Policy on Thursday 26 November 2026, setting out how requests to buy or take over council-owned land and property across the district will be judged. The report from the Director of Neighbourhood Services and Communities recommends that councillors approve it.

The policy sets out three routes: sale on the open market, sale to a special purchaser and Community Asset Transfer. Each request would go through stages including initial assessment, due diligence, an options appraisal, independent valuation and engagement before approval and legal completion, and the council could use restrictive covenants, overage and clawback clauses to protect its interests. Applicants or buyers would normally pay the council's legal and professional costs.

Requests would not normally go ahead if the council still needs the asset, if a substantially similar request was decided in the previous six months, or if the application fails the criteria. Any sale or lease of a large site would still need approval from Full Council, and the report says the financial effect of individual disposals would be set out in future reports.

councilwatch.headline: Auditors expect to give no opinion on three years of Basildon Council's accounts
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's external auditors, EY, told councillors that the 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26 accounts are all expected to receive disclaimed opinions, and listed borrowing, Sempra Homes and housing among areas of significant risk.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Audit and Risk Committee was told on Wednesday 4 November 2026 that all three sets of outstanding accounts, for 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26, are expected to receive disclaimed audit opinions. The update came from the council's external auditors, EY, according to the published minutes of the meeting. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor is unable to say whether the accounts give a true and fair view.

The minutes say the 2023/24 disclaimer follows statutory backstop arrangements that prevented audit work being completed. For 2024/25, councillors were told that despite substantial work by officers, not enough assurance had been obtained, and a partial audit report would be issued. For 2025/26, the minutes record that the council had been unable to adequately support the audit, with delays in providing evidence and problems with the quality of supporting documents, so only limited work will be done on areas including property valuations, loans and investments relating to the council's housing company Sempra Homes, and the Minimum Revenue Provision.

EY also set out significant risks for its value for money assessment, including the council's borrowing and financing costs, procurement and capital programme governance, Sempra Homes, internal control weaknesses, councillor conduct, and housing performance, including the council's C4 grading from the Regulator of Social Housing. Councillors were told several independent investigations commissioned by the council are still under way and will inform that assessment. The minutes say EY will consider whether to use formal statutory recommendations or other reporting powers once its work is complete.
points: 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26 accounts all expected to get disclaimed opinions

body: Basildon Borough Council's total borrowing stood at £727 million, including finance leases, at the end of September 2026, the council's Audit and Risk Committee heard on Wednesday 4 November 2026. Councillors discussed the council's investment property in Dartford and its effect on borrowing, and were told negotiations over its sale had been delayed, although a number of interested parties remained engaged. councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee was asked to say how it would have decided the Great Burstead scheme, after an appeal was lodged because no decision had been made. Officers backed the plan, which offers more than £20 million in contributions.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee considered an outline application for up to 910 homes on land at Foots Farm, Southend Road, Great Burstead, near Billericay, on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Because the applicant had already lodged an appeal on the grounds of non-determination, councillors were asked to indicate the decision they would have made had the application stayed with the council. Officers recommended that outline planning permission would have been granted.

The report says the 56.89 hectare site is farmland in the Metropolitan Green Belt and that the scheme counts as inappropriate development, but officers concluded its benefits significantly outweigh the harm. Half the homes would be affordable, with eight Gypsy and Traveller pitches, a community hub and 3.44 hectares safeguarded for a nursery and three-form entry primary school. The Section 106 package of more than £20 million covers education, healthcare, bus services, play and sports, and employment and skills, and the site forms part of the South East Billericay allocation in the emerging Basildon Local Plan.

Three residents and the chair of the parish council spoke against the plan, citing the loss of Green Belt and farmland, traffic on Coxes Farm Road and Bell Hill, and pressure on schools, GP services, water supply and drainage. Councillors also complained that a technical briefing had been arranged without consulting the committee's chair and vice-chair and without Essex County Council Highways, and it was agreed to seek Highways representation at future meetings. The application will now be settled through the appeal.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon scraps area planning committees and councillor call-in as new national rules take effect
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council now has one 13-member Planning Committee, with most applications decided by officers under a new national scheme of delegation.
body: Maldon District Council agreed on Thursday 22 October 2026 to set up a single Planning Committee of 13 members from Saturday 31 October 2026. It abolished the North Western, Central and South Eastern Area Planning Committees and the District Planning Committee on the same date. Councillors were told the change was required by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026, which came into force on 31 October.

Under the new National Scheme of Delegation, routine and minor applications go to officers, and larger or more sensitive ones are also delegated unless they pass a threshold known as the Gateway Test. There is no longer a process for councillors to call in applications. Councillor W Stamp said she did not consider the changes democratic and asked for her vote against to be recorded.

The new committee is due to meet every three weeks at 7pm, mostly on Wednesdays, with meetings cancelled when there is no business. A separate report to the same meeting proposed a revised public speaking protocol that would let ward councillors who do not sit on the committee speak on applications in their wards, raise speaking time from two to three minutes, and allow electronic voting.

body: Maldon District Council received a report from its Chief Executive on Thursday 22 October 2026 setting out what it spent preparing for a Mid Essex unitary council before the government paused local government reorganisation. Councillors agreed to ask for a full breakdown of the costs, including officer time, and details of how the Mid Essex Director was appointed.

The report says the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government withdrew the five-unitary model for Essex on 7 September 2026 and paused reorganisation for review. Costs between the choice of that model and the pause are estimated at £78,000, with Maldon expected to pay a third, about £26,000, for IT, a councillor engagement event, staff support and specialist project management. No posts were recruited specifically for the work, and earlier Freedom of Information requests about the costs were refused because the figures were due to be published.

The final figure is due to be confirmed by the Mid Essex Programme Board in November, and the council is still waiting to hear whether there are Essex-wide costs to share. Councillors were also told that Essex County Council has consented to a Greater Essex mayoral strategic authority with Southend-on-Sea City Council and Thurrock Council, though all three must agree, and that the first mayoral election is now planned for May 2028.

body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's cabinet held an extraordinary meeting on 5 November 2026 to consider the final draft of the city's new Local Plan. The papers say new criteria-based policies would give the council a more robust, evidenced approach to applications including Houses in Multiple Occupation, affordable housing and hot food takeaways. The meeting papers include the draft plan, a policies map, a report on the earlier Regulation 18 consultation, a sustainability appraisal and an updated Local Development Scheme setting out the timetable. Three questions from councillors were answered at the meeting and published with the minutes.

councilwatch.summary: Electrical safety checks on council homes are now close to complete, but councillors heard that repairs remain the weak spot in Southend's response to the social housing regulator.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Audit and Governance Committee received an update on 19 October 2026 on the council's progress in responding to a judgement by the Regulator of Social Housing. The report, from the Executive Director for Environment and Place, also covered the council's dealings with the Housing Ombudsman and the Building Safety Regulator.

The Head of Housing told the committee that monthly meetings with the regulator were continuing and that significant progress had been made on the council's Provider Improvement Plan. The council has reached 100% coverage of electrical safety checks in communal areas and 99% in homes, and the minutes say the regulator now regards electrical safety as business as usual. Repairs remain an area of focus, and a targeted improvement plan has been agreed with the council's repairs contractor to cut work in progress and bring performance up to industry norms by Christmas 2026.

Councillors were told the Housing Ombudsman's investigation has concluded, with the council due to submit a learning statement as the final stage. Officers said this was the first inspection under the new consumer regulation framework and that the council knew of areas needing improvement before the inspections took place. The committee asked for a further update on repairs performance.
points: Communal electrical safety check coverage: 100%; homes: 99%
Repairs contractor has a targeted improvement plan with a Christmas 2026 deadline
Housing Ombudsman investigation concluded; council to submit a learning statement
Committee asked for a further update on repairs

councilwatch.headline: Three in four Thurrock children entering care now get their first health check on time, up from 36%
councilwatch.summary: Councillors scrutinising children's services heard that initial health assessments within the 20-day legal deadline have more than doubled.
body: Thurrock Council's Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 22 October 2026 that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care are now completed within the statutory 20-day timescale. The figure compares with 36% previously, according to the minutes of the meeting.

Officers put the improvement down to closer joint working with Children's Services, more paediatric capacity and better oversight. They said late assessments were mainly caused by changes of placement, hospital admissions, missed appointments and occasional staff absence, and that only one delayed assessment in the reporting period was down to a lack of capacity.

The service is moving to a model led by specialist nurses working with paediatricians, and officers said a formal review in December 2026 will look at the views of children and families, the quality of assessments and timeliness. Councillors questioned whether enough paediatric capacity would remain, and officers said the aim was to use existing paediatric resources more effectively. The committee noted the update.
points: 75% of initial health assessments now within 20 days, up from 36%
Only one delay in the period was due to capacity
Formal review of the nurse-led model due in December 2026

councilwatch.headline: Epping Forest councillors asked to back raising the top fly-tipping fine from £1,000 to £5,000
councilwatch.summary: A motion to full council called for the district's maximum fixed penalty for fly-tipping to rise fivefold now that the law allows it.
body: A motion put to Epping Forest District Council's full council meeting on 22 October 2026 asked councillors to support, in principle, raising the council's maximum fixed penalty notice for fly-tipping from £1,000 to £5,000. It was proposed by Councillor K Rizvi and seconded by Councillor C McCann. The published papers do not yet record the outcome.

The motion says the council can currently issue fines of up to £1,000 for fly-tipping, but recent changes to the law now allow councils to set a maximum of £5,000. It argues that people who deliberately dump waste should face a penalty reflecting the damage to the environment and the costs borne by residents.

If backed, the motion asks the Cabinet Member for Environment and Regulatory Services to work with the council's environmental enforcement team to bring in the higher fine as soon as practicable, subject to legal and constitutional requirements. It also calls for clear public communication and continued enforcement, and encourages residents to keep reporting fly-tipping with photographs, CCTV or dashcam footage where they have it.
points: Current maximum fly-tipping fixed penalty: £1,000
Proposed maximum: £5,000
Motion considered at full council on 22 October 2026; outcome not yet published

councilwatch.headline: Tendring set to adopt new protection plans for St Osyth and Manningtree and Mistley conservation areas
councilwatch.summary: Cabinet will decide on 13 November whether to adopt the final two of 20 conservation area appraisals, including revised boundaries.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet will be asked on 13 November 2026 to adopt updated Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans for St Osyth and for Manningtree and Mistley. The report from the Portfolio Holder for Housing and Planning recommends adoption, including revised conservation area boundaries where applicable.

The report says both documents were shaped by public consultations held between 2022 and 2026, and that responses led to changes, including to some boundaries. Once adopted, the appraisals would become material planning considerations, meaning they would carry weight when planning applications in those areas are decided. They are the last two in a programme to review all 20 of the district's conservation areas, a priority of the Tendring Heritage Strategy, which includes five areas on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.

The report says that without adoption the council could not give weight to the updated appraisals in planning decisions, and its ability to conserve the district's historic environment would be reduced. The documents are also intended to inform the council's emerging Local Plan.
points: Cabinet decision due 13 November 2026
Covers St Osyth and Manningtree and Mistley, with revised boundaries where applicable
Completes the review of all 20 Tendring conservation areas

councilwatch.headline: Tendring adopts new skills and conduct standards for council housing staff after tenant feedback
councilwatch.summary: Cabinet adopted a policy setting out the skills, qualifications and conduct expected of housing staff, to meet a new regulator standard.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet adopted a Housing Competence and Conduct Policy on 23 October 2026. The policy sets out the knowledge, skills, experience and behaviour expected of council housing staff and contractors, and includes a Housing Code of Conduct for staff.

The report says the policy is needed to comply with the Regulator of Social Housing's Competence and Conduct Standard, which requires landlords to have a written policy, and that failing to meet it could expose the council to regulatory scrutiny and enforcement. It covers recruitment, training, professional qualifications, appraisal and performance management. Tenants told the council their priorities were being treated with respect, being listened to, getting an empathetic response and being kept informed.

Tenant consultation on the code of conduct closed on 28 October 2026, and the cabinet authorised the Corporate Director (Operations and Delivery) to make changes in response, in consultation with the housing portfolio holder. The policy will be reviewed annually and no later than October 2027.
points: Adopted by cabinet on 23 October 2026
Meets the Regulator of Social Housing's Competence and Conduct Standard
Review due no later than October 2027

councilwatch.headline: Tendring budgets for life beyond 2028 as the government pauses the council shake-up
councilwatch.summary: With Whitehall reviewing its plan to replace Essex's councils, Tendring's cabinet has agreed to plan four years ahead, and backed money for toilets, playgrounds and housing staff.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet has agreed to refresh the council's financial forecast over four years, to allow for the possibility that the council still exists after April 2028. That date had been the proposed start for a new unitary council under the government's original timetable for Greater Essex, but on 7 September 2026 the government announced it would pause and review its local government reorganisation programme.

The report to cabinet on 23 October said the pause had brought a significant level of uncertainty for the councils affected, though Tendring's two-year financial plan still left it in a positive position. If reorganisation goes ahead, even later than planned, the forecast can be switched back to the council's earlier approach of preparing for a handover to the new authority.

Cabinet also approved changes to this year's budget, including £540,000 for housing capacity and restructuring, £100,000 to invest in public toilets and £400,000 for project delivery capacity, and accepted £270,000 from the government's Playground Fund. The report said the general fund was £3.669m underspent against its profiled budget at the end of July, largely because of the timing of spending.
points: Forecast to be refreshed over four years in case the council continues beyond April 2028
Government paused its reorganisation programme on 7 September 2026
£270,000 Playground Fund grant accepted and £100,000 set aside for public toilets
General fund £3.669m underspent at the end of July, mostly down to timing
